A discrete random variable has an expectation only when both positive and negative parts are finite.
If the expectation of X is finite, then X is integrable.
If the expectation of Y is finite, then Y is integrable.
For real-valued integrable variables, the triangle inequality applies.
The absolute value of the sum is at most the sum of absolute values.
Therefore the expected absolute value of X plus Y is finite.
Hence the expectation of X plus Y is defined and finite.
This holds for any discrete probability space.
It does not require independence.
It does not require bounded support.
The finite expectations already control the tails.
A counterexample cannot exist in the standard theory.
Some informal calculations use conditional sums.
Those informal sums can rearrange or cancel terms.
That is not the usual expectation definition.
The Lebesgue or summable expectation requires absolute integrability.
For discrete variables, absolute integrability means absolute summability.
If X and Y are absolutely summable, their sum is absolutely summable.
This is a basic property of integrable functions.
Thus the requested phenomenon does not occur.
The answer is simply no.
Under the standard definition of expectation for discrete random variables finite first moments of both variables together always clearly and carefully with standard care keep the sum safely in every ordinary probability model beneath the usual integrability barrier.
